brand_model: Cole-Parmer sterilizing air filter, 0.2 um hydrophobic PTFE, 50 mm
key_specs: ALREADY IN THE LAB - listed so a replicator can buy one. Hydrophobic PTFE membrane in a PP housing, 0.2 um, 50 mm disc, 16.2 cm2 effective area, supplied sterile. Stepped hose barb for 1/4 to 3/8 in (6-9.5 mm) ID tubing, so it needs a step down to the 4 mm line the riser takes. Max 60 psi / 4.1 bar - fifteen times the 3.9 psi the registered pump can dead-head, so pressure rating is not a constraint here. Autoclavable 30 cycles at 121 C / 20 min, or 3 at 134 C / 30 min, which this build does not need since it is chemically sterilised. PRESSURE DROP IS THE SPEC THAT MATTERS AND COLE-PARMER PUBLISH NONE. head() carries 3.45 kPa per L/min as sparge_filter_drop_slope - EXTRAPOLATED from an equivalent 0.2 um PTFE disc of near-identical dimensions, NOT measured. That is 14.1 kPa at the 4.09 L/min design point, twelve times the vessel back-pressure and over half of what the metering valve would otherwise have had to drop. Area-correcting Pall Acro 50 to 16.2 cm2 gives 3.02, so the figure used is 14 % conservative of the best-documented comparable part. Measure it with a water manometer and replace the number - see TODO.md. Price is CAD 204.65 per pack of 10 on the Cole-Parmer Canada listing; the unit_price_usd column carries that CAD figure unconverted.

brand_model: 316 stainless welded tube, 4 mm OD x 0.5 mm wall (3 mm ID), hard temper
key_specs: STOCK LENGTH, cut to make two tubes: the sparger feed riser and its support tube, 186.7 mm each as drawn - 15 mm proud of the port for a hose clamp, down to 8 mm inside the socket. 373.4 mm total, so the model asks for a 500 mm length; buying the 1 m at 22.72 rather than the 0.5 m at 13.28 leaves 626 mm spare - enough to remake both twice and to feed the bent-tube sparger variant in TODO. WELDED, not seamless: at 4 mm OD the seamless equivalent is 181.42/m against 22.72, is SOFT temper where a support tube wants hard, and comes only in a 1 mm wall so a 2 mm bore. The weld bead costs nothing here - the riser drops a few hundred Pa against the 24 kPa the metering valve burns, and the support tube is a dead leg by design, which is a worse crevice than a bead either way. 4 x 2.5 mm, which this row used to name, is not a size anyone sells. 316 because it is wetted and stays in the culture. The support one is capped at the ring and takes a drilled hole or filed slit at whatever height its own job wants. Deburr the ID after cutting - a wheel cutter rolls a 0.5 mm wall inward.

brand_model: Dwyer VFA-23 acrylic variable-area flow meter, 0.6-5 L/min air, no valve
key_specs: Closes the measured-gas-flow gap. 0.1-0.5 vvm on 8.17 L is 0.82-4.09 L/min, so the design point sits at 81.7% of a 5 L/min scale and 0.1 vvm at 16.3% - both on scale, which is what a 0-5 range buys. THE SCALE READS L/MIN, and only one other candidate did: everything McMaster sells in this range reads scfh, where the design point is 8.66 of them and every reading in the paper carries a conversion. CALIBRATION BASIS IS THE SPEC THAT DECIDED IT - Dwyer bulletin F-33 gives 14.7 psia and 70 F, which is this regime, so the correction at the line back-pressure is 0.7%. The medical channel is referenced at 50 psig and the welding channel at 30, which would read 87% wrong here, and that ruled both out entirely rather than on price. Accuracy is 5% of FULL SCALE, so 0.25 L/min, which is 6.1% at the design point; Cole-Parmer have no 5 L/min rung and their nearest tube is 8.5 full scale, costing 10.4% at the same point for 69% more money. THIS IS THE BARE METER. VFA-23-BV carries an integral brass valve whose Cv Dwyer do not publish, so the throttle is a separate characterised part instead - see the metering valve row - and that valve goes UPSTREAM of this meter, which is what the 0.7% correction assumes. Nickel-plated brass body, acrylic block, 1/8 NPT female back or end connection, so it needs NPT-to-barb adapters at both ends. Graduation interval is not published anywhere; over a 70 mm scale it resolves finer than the 0.25 L/min accuracy, so it is worth asking Dwyer but does not block ordering. Price is CAD 86.22 and the unit_price_usd column carries it unconverted, same as the filter row. See working.tmp/BOM-OPTIONS.md for the eight rejected candidates.

brand_model: Clippard MNV-4K2 miniature needle valve, 1/8 in hose barb, knurled knob
key_specs: The throttle, and it sits UPSTREAM of the rotameter so the meter sees only downstream line loss. Required Cv is 0.0296 at the 4.087 L/min design point: the pump would give 28.1 L/min against this line, so the valve drops 9.96 kPa on top of the line own 15.34. Cv 0.090 is 3.0x that, putting the design point at 33% of wide open - inside the 2-4x band that keeps the setting mid-travel rather than against a stop. THIS ANSWER MOVED WHEN THE FILTER WAS COUNTED. On the old budget the throttle dropped 24.2 kPa for a required Cv of 0.020 and the pick was MNV-2 at Cv 0.032; the sterile filter own 14.1 kPa cut the throttle share to 9.96 and raised required Cv to 0.0296, which leaves MNV-2 at 92% of wide open with no control authority, and Ideal Valve 52-1-12 at Cv 0.019 unable to reach the flow at all - 156%. Brass body, stainless stem, nitrile seal, rated 5 scfm at 100 psig, far above anything here. 1/8 in hose barb both ends fits the 4 mm silicone line directly and it is the only barbed candidate in the set. Clippard publish a flow-vs-turns chart for MNV-1/2/3/4 at catalog p.153, so resolution is documentable rather than assumed; the MNV-4 needle angle is not in our notes and is worth reading off that chart, and MNV-1 is the 15 degree coarse one to avoid. See working.tmp/GAS-CHAIN-LEADS.md section 3c for the rejected candidates.

brand_model: Cole-Parmer miniature check valve, polypropylene body, Viton diaphragm, 3/16 in barb
key_specs: Stops culture siphoning back into the pump when it stops. Sits between the metering valve and the sterile filter. 0.18 psi cracking / 0.014 psi closing, published; Cv 0.12. REAL COST TO THE LINE IS 1.85 kPa - 1.24 of cracking plus 0.61 of flowing drop at the 4.087 L/min design point. The flowing half is never on a spec sheet and is what separates otherwise-identical parts: an Air Logic umbrella at the same nominal cracking pressure costs 0.9 kPa more because its flow capacity is a quarter of this one. 3/16 in barb is +19 % stretch on 4 mm ID silicone airline. Barb size barely affects flow here - Cole-Parmer publish Cv per size and it only moves 0.11 to 0.13 across 1/8 to 5/16 - so the barb is chosen to fit the tube, not to chase pressure. CHOSEN ON PROCUREMENT, NOT PHYSICS: US Plastic 22577 is 1.78 kPa, a 4 % difference, which is inside the error on the filter figure that dominates the budget. Same supplier as the sterile filter 1594522 means one shipment, one account, one customs clearance into Canada. Viton rather than the nylon/silicone sibling 5011519: nylon is hygroscopic and swells in continuously humid air. CONFIRM BEFORE ORDERING: the page reads "Working Pressure 3-5 psi" while the pump dead-heads at 3.9 psi and the valve runs at about 2.2 psig in service, so it sits below that band normally and at it on dead-head. The 0.014 psi closing pressure argues it seals fine at low pressure, but the wording is ambiguous. See working.tmp/BOM-OPTIONS.md for the other 12 candidates and why each was rejected.

brand_model: McMaster compact metal tube and conduit cutter, 1/8 to 7/8 in OD
key_specs: Cuts the 316 SS riser stock into 2 x 187 mm. RATED FOR STAINLESS, which is the filter that rules out most cheap tube cutters - many are copper and aluminium only. 1/8 to 7/8 in OD, so the 4 mm (0.157 in) tube sits just above the minimum. Steel cutting wheel, grooved rollers, 1.5 in swing radius, 2 5/8 in long. Replacement wheels sold separately. IT DOES NOT DEBURR. A wheel cutter rolls material inward at the cut and the riser bore is only 3 mm, with that restriction landing exactly where gas enters - so an inside deburring tool is a separate row and a required assembly step, not a nicety. Noga RC1000 (3-5.5 mm) is the only tool found whose range brackets a 3 mm bore. A jeweller''s saw in a mitre jig is the alternative worth considering: a wheel cutter always rolls a thin wall inward, a saw does not, which removes the problem at source rather than fixing it after. Listed REACH and RoHS non-compliant - irrelevant here, it is a bench tool and never enters the reactor, unlike the wetted parts this project does hold to those standards.
